content.text:
Cleaned up my tmux socket (`-L uirev174`, `-L uirev174b`; never a bare `kill-server` on the default socket). No files modified — the working tree diff is byte-identical to what I was handed (327 lines).

## 1. Verdict

**Acceptable as-is.** The reworded line is correct in every shape I could produce, and — the thing most worth checking — the sizes it offers are *honest*: I grew a window to each offered pair and the panels came up. `Grow to 190x30` at a 100x30 window with `COLUMNS=190`, `Grow to 100x40` in the mixed tolerated-width case (`LINES=40 COLUMNS=80`), and even `Grow to 512x512` under `LINES=99999 COLUMNS=99999` all bring the full-screen display up. The worst case measures 61 columns and prints only in windows of at least 72, so nothing wraps at 72x24 or 80x24. The three round-1 findings are genuinely answered: the unset-only quote no longer leads either manual, "rerun" now rides with the unset half alone and I confirmed by hand that growing to the offered size is taken at the next "play again" *in the same process* with no rerun, and the branch correctly declines to offer a size when any named axis is under the floor (`LINES=40 COLUMNS=60` at 100x30 still gets the unset-only line, which is the right answer since no window is wide enough for a `COLUMNS` of 60). What is left are three nits, none of which should hold the change.

## 2. Findings

**Nit — the grow half never says when it takes effect.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`, the new `proutf`. Of the four advice lines a player can meet, this is the only one whose primary action has no timing attached. Its nearest sibling is explicit — `Grow the terminal to 72x24 and the next game gets panels.` — and the unset half of the new line carries `rerun sst -t`, so the grow half is conspicuously the one clause with no "and then what". A player who reads `Grow to 190x30` at startup, grows the window, and keeps playing sees nothing happen for the whole game. Both manuals now say growing is answered at the next "play again"; the line does not, and I do not think it can: `Grow to 190x30 for panels next game, ...` takes the worst case to 81 columns, well past the 72 the line has to live in. The retry notice at play-again does close the loop (I saw it print again after a partial grow to 150x30). Suggestion: accept the gap, but record it deliberately — a sentence in the existing comment saying the timing was cut for width, not overlooked, so the next reader does not "fix" it by adding it back.

**Nit — "that size" in both manuals is not the size the line prints.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md` (~line 121) and `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.doc` (~line 1573), both reading "it is taken as soon as the window catches up with it, so the game offers you that size as well". The line does not offer the pin's size; it offers the size the *window* would have to reach, which is the larger of the two per axis. In the mixed shape I drove — `LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` in a 100x30 window — the player sees three different pairs stacked:

```
Terminal is 100x30 but LINES/COLUMNS make it 80x40.
Grow to 100x40, or unset LINES and rerun sst -t.
```

`100x40` is neither the window nor the pinned pair, and a reader who came to the manual to understand the notice has been prepared for only two of the three numbers. The advice itself is right — telling them `80x40` would ask them to narrow a window already wide enough — and the tests carry that reasoning; it is only the manual sentence that under-describes it. Suggestion: "so the game offers the size the window would have to reach as well". That is one clause, costs no accuracy, and covers the mixed case without the manuals having to spell it out.

**Nit — the missing comma in the worst-case line is right, and looks like an oversight.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`. At `LINES=99999 COLUMNS=99999` the line reads:

```
Grow to 512x512, or unset LINES and COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.
```

Three `and`s unbroken, where the sibling compound form punctuates the identical clause — `Grow to 72x24, unset LINES and COLUMNS, and rerun sst -t.` I think the omission is correct and should stay: a comma before "and rerun" would let the rerun read as applying to the grow half too, which is exactly the error round 2 removed. But that makes it a trap. The comment explains why the rerun rides with the unset half; it does not explain why the punctuation that would normally mark that clause is absent, so the next person to notice the inconsistency with the line above will add the comma back and undo the fix. Suggestion: one clause in the existing comment tying the absent comma to the same reason.

**Observation, not a finding against this change.** At the play-again retry the notice butts against the prompt with no separator: `Do you want to play again?Terminal is 150x30 but LINES/COLUMNS make it 190x30.` The play-again prompt does not end its line and the answer is not echoed there — the same run-on appears in plain mode with no `-t` involved (`Do you want to play again?Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?`). Pre-existing on `main`; this change alters only the line beneath it. Mentioning it so it is not attributed here; if it is worth an issue, that is a separate slice.

One arithmetic note on round 1's resolved nit 3, for the record only: the reasoning given was that `Grow the window to` would put the worst case at 71 of 72 columns. By my count the prefix grows by 11 characters, so the worst case lands at exactly 72 in a 72-column window — which strengthens rather than weakens the resolution, since a 72-character line fills the row completely. The elision in `Grow to` is justified, and the surrounding `Terminal is ...` line supplies the missing noun.

## 3. What I exercised

All in tmux on my own sockets, `-f /dev/null -L uirev174` / `-L uirev174b`, against `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/build/debug/sst`.

Notice shapes captured at startup: `COLUMNS=190` at 100x30 (new line, 50 cols); `LINES=40` at 100x30 (new line, 48 cols); `LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` at 100x30 (mixed/tolerated-width, `Grow to 100x40` against a `make it 80x40` report); `LINES=40 COLUMNS=60` at 100x30 (correctly falls back to unset-only); `LINES=20` at 100x30 and `COLUMNS=190 LINES=20` at 100x30 (under-floor pins, unset-only, one and both axes named); `COLUMNS=75` at 70x20 (compound form unchanged); bare 70x20 (no-pin small-window pair unchanged); `COLUMNS=80` at 100x30 (tolerated pin, no notice, panels up).

Width and wrap: the worst case `LINES=99999 COLUMNS=99999` at both 72x24 and 80x24 — curses clamps to 512 as the comment claims, the line renders at 61 columns on one row with eleven to spare at 72, no wrap or truncation. Measured every advice line's length; the new family runs 48/50/61 against existing siblings at 57.

Honesty of the offered sizes: grew a pane to 190x30 with `COLUMNS=190` and answered yes at play-again — panels came up in the same process, no rerun, which is the claim the new wording rests on; started fresh at 100x40 with `LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` — panels; started at 512x512 with both pins at 99999 — panels.

Retry journey: full `regular/short/novice/xyz/quit` game at 100x30 under `COLUMNS=190`, resized to 150x30 mid-prompt, answered yes — the size report updated to `Terminal is 150x30` and the new advice line reprinted, then the same journey resized to 190x30 instead and the panels came up.

Regressions: unpinned 72x24 draws the panels normally; the scripted plain-mode journey `regular/short/novice/xyz/srscan/quit/n` is unaffected (no `-t`, so `refusal_notice()` never runs).

content.content:
title:	proutf() is named like prout() but behaves like proutn(): it does not end its line
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	
comments:	0
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	162
--
## Problem

The three output helpers in `sst.c` pair up by name, but not by
behaviour:

| function | ends the line? |
| --- | --- |
| `proutn(s)` | no |
| `prout(s)` | **yes** -- it is literally `proutn(s); skip(1);` |
| `proutf(fmt, ...)` | **no** |

`prout` is `proutn` plus a newline, so the natural reading of `proutf`
is "`prout` with a format". It is not: it ends with

```c
	if (*p != '\0') proutn(p);
```

so a format string with no trailing `\n` leaves the line open. The
formatted counterpart of `prout` does not exist, and the one that does
is named as though it were.

## Why it matters

It misleads, and it has. While implementing #154 I replaced a `prout`
with a `proutf` to interpolate two numbers into a notice, and the notice
ran into the question after it:

```
Terminal is 80x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.Would you like a regular, tourn
ament, or frozen game?
```

That reached a review round before a test caught it -- and caught it
sideways, by failing on the *wrapped question* rather than on the
notice.

It is visible in shipped output too. The end-of-game questions share a
line for the same reason (`sst.c:528` and `sst.c:534` are both `proutf`
with no `\n`):

```
Do you want your score recorded?Do you want to play again?
```

gh issue comment 162 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
One refinement to the "visible in shipped output too" evidence, measured
today on this branch's build (plain mode, no `-t`, in a 100x30 tmux pane):

The end-of-game pair only runs together when the answer arrives before
the prompt does. With the player waiting for the question, the terminal's
own echo of the Enter ends the line and the display is fine:

```
Do you want your score recorded?n
Do you want to play again?
```

Send the `n` ahead of the prompt -- typeahead, or any piped stdin, which
is how `tests/golden.sh` and the scripted plain-mode journey in AGENTS.md
see it -- and the echo lands somewhere earlier, so the two questions
concatenate exactly as the issue shows:

```
Do you want your score recorded?Do you want to play again?
```

So the shipped-output symptom is real but conditional: it is the echo
that has been ending those lines, not the game. That makes it worse for
the recordings and the test journeys than for a player at a normal pace,
and it means a change that stops relying on the echo cannot be validated
by watching an interactive session.

Found while checking a `ui-review` observation on the branch for #174
(the notice running into the play-again prompt at the retry), which turns
out to be the same conditional shape rather than a separate defect.
EOF
)"

input.command:
gh issue create --title "Eleven CRLF source files are unprotected by .gitattributes, and a whole-file flip is invisible to every check" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

Eleven tracked files are entirely CRLF, and every one of them is a file
the build compiles or the game reads:

```
ai.c  battle.c  events.c  finish.c  moving.c  planets.c
reports.c  setup.c  sst.c  sst.h  sst.doc
```

(Measured with `grep -c $'\r'` against the line count: all lines, not
some.) The newer files -- `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tuifmt.c`, `rules.c`,
`rules.h`, `osx.c`, `osx.h` -- are LF, so the tree is mixed by vintage.

`.gitattributes` covers only `tests/golden/*.txt`:

```
# The golden fixtures are compared byte for byte, so a clone that
# rewrote their line endings would fail every journey.
tests/golden/*.txt -text
```

The reasoning in that comment applies to the eleven as well, and stops
one directory short of them.

## Why it matters

A wholesale line-ending flip in any of those files passes every check
this repository has. The compiler does not care: I flipped all 1130
lines of `sst.c` to LF by accident and the `verifier` rebuilt both
`ci-*` presets and compared disassembly -- `.text` byte-identical in
Debug and Release, zero warnings under `-Werror`. `ctest` passes, the
journeys pass, the golden recordings pass, `analyze` passes. The only
thing that shows it is `git diff --stat`, where `sst.c` read 2314
changed lines instead of 58.

Two ways it gets in:

- **A clone that normalizes.** With no `text` attribute git falls back
  to `core.autocrlf`, which is `true` by default in Git for Windows.
  Checked out and committed back, all eleven files flip -- about 8,700
  lines across a diff nobody can review.
- **An editing tool in text mode.** Python's `open(p).read()` /
  `open(p, "w").write()` strips CRLF silently, and so does any editor
  configured to normalize on save. This is how it happened here, on the
  branch for #174; it was caught by reading `git diff --stat` and not
  by anything automatic.

Either way the damage is a diff that looks like a rewrite, or -- worse
-- a real change buried in one, since the genuine hunks are
indistinguishable from the noise once the whole file has moved.

## Where it was found

While preparing the branch for #174 (the oversize-pin refusal notice).
Two comment edits to `sst.c` made with a text-mode script stripped the
file's line endings; the `verifier` had flagged only that `sst.c` was
edited mid-run, and its `.text` comparison correctly reported the
binaries identical, which is exactly why nothing else noticed.

## Fixing it

Add the eleven to `.gitattributes` with their actual ending, so git
stops guessing and a clone on any platform gets them back byte for
byte. Something like:

```
*.c  -text
*.h  -text
sst.doc -text
```

-- except that `-text` on `*.c` would also freeze the LF files, which
is the right outcome but should be stated deliberately rather than
inherited. Per-file `eol=crlf` for the eleven is the narrower option.

Worth deciding at the same time whether a check belongs in CI. A
`git diff --check`-style guard, or a test that asserts each of the
eleven still has no bare LF, would turn the silent case into a failing
one. That is the part the golden-fixture line above does not have
either.
EOF
)"

## Verdict: **approve**

Approval covers the exact state I reviewed: branch `fix/oversize-pin-notice` at `HEAD = 6f538a9` with nothing staged, nothing untracked, and six modified files — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c`, `tui.h`, `sst.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md`, `sst.doc` (`git diff main` is the whole change). The three findings below are comment-only; if you fix any of them the reviewed state changes and step 11 asks for a fresh (cheap) round.

---

## Findings

### should-fix

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:487`** — the sentence now contradicts the paragraph 19 lines below it.

`The three that carry numbers get no column count here.` is followed, in the same comment block, by `The grow-or-unset line added for #174 is the third, and it does get a count ... 61 columns`. Everything in the paragraph the first sentence introduces (the "five attempts were wrong" reasoning, the fifteen-columns-inside result, the "under 72 it cannot pass 52" result) is about the size report and the retry line only — the two. A reader takes the opening sentence as spec, and it is false for the third line.

Failure scenario: the next person to touch this line reads "no column count here", believes there is no stated bound to keep true, and changes the wording past 61 columns without re-deriving anything.

Suggested fix: restore `The two that carry numbers get no column count here.` (the size report and the retry line) and let the following paragraph introduce the third as the one that *can* be bounded — or reword to `Three lines carry numbers. Two of them get no column count here:`.

### nit

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:510`** — `tui_refusal_growable() prints nothing where an axis is under the floor` makes the function the subject of "prints"; it prints nothing under any circumstances, it returns `FALSE`. Suggest `answers FALSE where an axis is under the floor`, which is also what makes the "so both are then oversize" step follow.

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:1195-1232`** — the 38-line doc block headed `Whether a pinned dimension is what refused the player, and which.` now sits immediately above `oversize()` rather than above `blames()`, which is what it describes; only its last paragraph (1227-1232) is about the split. A reader arriving at `oversize()` gets a header that is not about it. Suggest moving the "The two halves are named…" paragraph to its own short header above `oversize()`/`underfloor()` and keeping the rest attached to `blames()`.

---

## Review coverage (`ui-review`)

The diff plainly reaches the player, and the pass ran twice with a coverage list that names journeys the change actually reaches (the four advice forms and the 61-column both-axes line). I agree with your judgment that the post-round-2 edits did not need a third round, and I checked it rather than took it: the only player-visible strings the diff introduces or alters are the four `proutf`/`prout` advice lines and the two size-report lines in `refusal_notice()`, and I drove all six live (see below) — they are byte-identical to the text quoted in the manuals and in your round-2 account. The manual edits made after round 2 are not player-visible in-game: the block you changed sits under "Modifications I made:" at `sst.doc:1562`, which is not a help topic, and `README.md` is not read by the game at all.

Limit on that: I can only compare the final state against your description of what round 2 saw. The intermediate states are not in git, so "no printed line changed after round 2" is verified as far as the final artefact allows and no further.

---

## What I verified independently

- **CRLF integrity** (you asked me to check this rather than take your word). Per file, working tree vs `HEAD`: `sst.c` 1184/1184 lines CR-terminated (HEAD 1130/1130), `sst.doc` 1714/1714 (HEAD 1709/1709), and `README.md`, `tests/tui.sh`, `tui.c`, `tui.h` contain zero CR bytes anywhere. No mixed lines, no missing final newline, every file matches HEAD's convention. (`git diff --check` flags the CRLF files as "trailing whitespace" — that is the CR, and it does the same on HEAD, so it is not a finding.)
- **Build**: `gcc -std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -O2` on `tui.c` and `sst.c` — clean, including `-Wmaybe-uninitialized` over the `needcols`/`needrows` pair, which are only read under the short-circuited `blame != NULL && tui_refusal_growable(...)`.
- **The 512 clamp** the 61-column bound rests on: `COLUMNS=99999 tput cols` → 512, `COLUMNS=513` → 512, `COLUMNS=511` → 511. And the worst case end-to-end, at 72x24 with both pinned to 99999: the game printed `Grow to 512x512, or unset LINES and COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.` at exactly 61 columns, eleven inside the window. The 38-char fixed text, the 59/82 figures for the rejected "for panels next game" wording, and the "75 unclamped" figure (two 10-digit `int`-max pins, which is what `pinned()` admits) all recompute correctly.
- **`tui_refusal_growable()` against `tui_init()`'s gate**, by hand over every shape and live under tmux on a private socket (`-L crev`, `-f /dev/null`, killed after): the per-axis max is right where the pinned pair is wrong (`LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` at 100x30 reports `make it 80x40` and correctly advises `Grow to 100x40`), the under-the-floor veto fires on the mixed shape (`LINES=40 COLUMNS=60` → unset-only), and both `MINROWS`/`MINCOLS` clamps are genuinely unreachable from `sst.c`'s `!smallwindow` caller, as your `tui.c` comment states. I also confirmed the offered size is actually *accepted*: `LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` in a 100x40 window brings the panels up with no notice.
- **Every literal in `tests/tui.sh`** — the three new arms, the rewritten "oversize LINES" arm and the two `scrollback_count` retry literals — matched against live game output character for character, including the retry sizes (150x30 with `COLUMNS=190` and 100x35 with `LINES=40` print exactly the strings those arms count, and identically to their startup notices, so the `-lt 2` counts still mean what they say). The three surviving old arms (`undersize pin`, `pin equal to the window`, the 3609 compound check) still take the branches their comments claim.
- Line widths: the new `sst.doc` block wraps at ≤69, matching the surrounding text; `tui.h`'s new entry matches `tui_refused_sizes`'s layout exactly.

## What I could not review

- The full `ctest` battery, both `ci-*` presets, the golden recordings and the complete `tests/tui.sh` run — the `verifier`'s scope, and it reports both configurations clean. I did not re-run them.
- The intermediate worktree states the two `ui-review` rounds saw, as above.
- Your mutation proofs, which ran on copies outside the repository; the two breaks you name (`needcols = refusedtermcols` unconditionally, and dropping the under-the-floor test) do map onto arms that would catch them — the "both axes oversize" and "pinned axis" arms for the first, "oversize height with an undersize width" for the second — which is consistent with what you reported.

## Verdict: **approve**

Approval covers the exact state I reviewed: branch `fix/oversize-pin-notice` at `HEAD = 6f538a9` with nothing staged, nothing untracked, and six modified files — `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c`, `tui.h`, `sst.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md`, `sst.doc` (`git diff main` is the whole change). The three findings below are comment-only; if you fix any of them the reviewed state changes and step 11 asks for a fresh (cheap) round.

---

## Findings

### should-fix

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:487`** — the sentence now contradicts the paragraph 19 lines below it.

`The three that carry numbers get no column count here.` is followed, in the same comment block, by `The grow-or-unset line added for #174 is the third, and it does get a count ... 61 columns`. Everything in the paragraph the first sentence introduces (the "five attempts were wrong" reasoning, the fifteen-columns-inside result, the "under 72 it cannot pass 52" result) is about the size report and the retry line only — the two. A reader takes the opening sentence as spec, and it is false for the third line.

Failure scenario: the next person to touch this line reads "no column count here", believes there is no stated bound to keep true, and changes the wording past 61 columns without re-deriving anything.

Suggested fix: restore `The two that carry numbers get no column count here.` (the size report and the retry line) and let the following paragraph introduce the third as the one that *can* be bounded — or reword to `Three lines carry numbers. Two of them get no column count here:`.

### nit

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:510`** — `tui_refusal_growable() prints nothing where an axis is under the floor` makes the function the subject of "prints"; it prints nothing under any circumstances, it returns `FALSE`. Suggest `answers FALSE where an axis is under the floor`, which is also what makes the "so both are then oversize" step follow.

**`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:1195-1232`** — the 38-line doc block headed `Whether a pinned dimension is what refused the player, and which.` now sits immediately above `oversize()` rather than above `blames()`, which is what it describes; only its last paragraph (1227-1232) is about the split. A reader arriving at `oversize()` gets a header that is not about it. Suggest moving the "The two halves are named…" paragraph to its own short header above `oversize()`/`underfloor()` and keeping the rest attached to `blames()`.

---

## Review coverage (`ui-review`)

The diff plainly reaches the player, and the pass ran twice with a coverage list that names journeys the change actually reaches (the four advice forms and the 61-column both-axes line). I agree with your judgment that the post-round-2 edits did not need a third round, and I checked it rather than took it: the only player-visible strings the diff introduces or alters are the four `proutf`/`prout` advice lines and the two size-report lines in `refusal_notice()`, and I drove all six live (see below) — they are byte-identical to the text quoted in the manuals and in your round-2 account. The manual edits made after round 2 are not player-visible in-game: the block you changed sits under "Modifications I made:" at `sst.doc:1562`, which is not a help topic, and `README.md` is not read by the game at all.

Limit on that: I can only compare the final state against your description of what round 2 saw. The intermediate states are not in git, so "no printed line changed after round 2" is verified as far as the final artefact allows and no further.

---

## What I verified independently

- **CRLF integrity** (you asked me to check this rather than take your word). Per file, working tree vs `HEAD`: `sst.c` 1184/1184 lines CR-terminated (HEAD 1130/1130), `sst.doc` 1714/1714 (HEAD 1709/1709), and `README.md`, `tests/tui.sh`, `tui.c`, `tui.h` contain zero CR bytes anywhere. No mixed lines, no missing final newline, every file matches HEAD's convention. - **Build**: `gcc -std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -O2` on `tui.c` and `sst.c` — clean, including `-Wmaybe-uninitialized` over the `needcols`/`needrows` pair, which are only read under the short-circuited `blame != NULL && tui_refusal_growable(...)`.

state:	OPEN

## Problem

`CMakeLists.txt` sets a 300-second timeout on the `tui` test and
explains it with:

> The timeout is far above the ~11s it takes to pass

Measured: **51s** on `main`, and **68s** after #88 adds squeeze cases.
The claim is out by roughly six times, and every branch that adds a
session to `tests/tui.sh` widens the gap.

# Verdict: approve

Reviewed state: branch `fix/oversize-pin-notice` at HEAD `6f538a9` with six modified, unstaged files (`README.md`, `sst.c`, `sst.doc`, `tests/tui.sh`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`; +344/−30; working-diff sha1 `91ae6a197154`). No staged changes, no untracked files. Approval is valid only for this exact state.

## What I verified independently (not taken on your word)

**Line endings.** `sst.c` is 1185 lines, 1185 CRLF, 1185 CR total, zero lone CRs, final byte pair `\r\n`; `sst.doc` likewise (1714/1714). `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md` are wholly LF. The `git diff main` hunks for `sst.c` are only the intended ones — a whole-file EOL flip would have rewritten every line — so the restoration is complete. The `git diff --check` "trailing whitespace" noise on `sst.c`/`sst.doc` is just the CR in a CRLF file and is pre-existing, not introduced.

**The printed lines, live.** Drove `build/ci-debug/sst` (built 12:22, newer than both changed C files) under tmux on my own socket (`-L rvw`, `-f /dev/null`), 100x30:

- `COLUMNS=190` → `Grow to 190x30, or unset COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.`
- `LINES=40 COLUMNS=80` → `Grow to 100x40, or unset LINES and rerun sst -t.` (the larger-per-axis rule, not the report's `80x40`)
- `LINES=40 COLUMNS=190` → `Grow to 190x40, or unset LINES and COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.` (60 columns)
- `LINES=40 COLUMNS=60` → `Unset LINES and COLUMNS, rerun sst -t -- classic for now.` (unset-only preserved under a floor-blamed axis)
- `LINES=99999 COLUMNS=99999` → `Grow to 512x512, or unset LINES and COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.` — exactly the 61 columns `sst.c:508` claims, and the worst case is reachable.

Every one matches the `fallback` arm strings and both manuals byte for byte.

**The 512 clamp the 61-column bound rests on.** Built a standalone ncurses probe (`initscr()`, print `LINES`/`COLS`) against the system ncurses 6.6.20251231 and ran it on a pty with `LINES=99999 COLUMNS=99999`: `LINES=512 COLS=512`. The three-digit premise holds, and the fixed-text arithmetic checks out (38 fixed + 17 blame + 3 + 3 = 61; the rejected "for panels next game" variant is 59 fixed → 82, as stated).

**"Meeting the pin" end to end.** Reproduced the arm by hand: refused at 100x30 with `COLUMNS=190`, `quit`/`n` to the play-again prompt, `resize-window -x 190 -y 30`, `y` — panels up in the same process, and `capture-pane -p -S -` returned **1** occurrence of `LINES/COLUMNS make it`. So your correction of the earlier version is right on both counts: counting the advice line would indeed pass with the panels down (a de-blamed pin prints the report alone), and tmux does keep the pre-alternate history — `screen_alternate_on()` copies the visible rows into `saved_grid` and clears on the *same* grid, so the scrollback survives. The comment at `tests/tui.sh:3814-3823` is correct and does not contradict the older note at `tests/tui.sh:134-137`, which is about content written *while* on the alt screen.

**Whole file green.** `tests/tui.sh build/ci-ebug/sst Debug` — sorry, `tests/tui.sh build/ci-debug/sst Debug` — exits 0, `tui OK`, zero FAIL lines, in this exact worktree. `sh -n` and `shellcheck -s sh` clean. `gcc -std=gnu17 -O2 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -c` on both `sst.c` and `tui.c` is clean, so the uninitialized `needcols`/`needrows` on the FALSE path draws no `-Wmaybe-uninitialized` at optimisation.

**The logic, case by case.** `tui_refusal_growable()`'s offered size is exactly sufficient in every reachable shape: the oversize axis's pin is ≥ the floor (else `underfloor` would have returned FALSE), and the non-oversize axis is either a tolerated pin ≤ the window or the window itself. The two floor clamps also produce a correct answer for the hypothetical smallwindow caller (70x20 with `COLUMNS=75` → 75x24, which really is accepted). `oversize()` implies pinned, since `tui_init()` `resize_term()`s a free axis to the ioctl's value and `term_v != 0` implies `haveterm`.

## Findings

**Nit — `tui.h:85-90`:** the header says growable answers "FALSE where no window is big enough", which is untrue of the ordinary too-small terminal. At 70x20 with nothing exported, neither axis is oversize, so the function returns FALSE — yet growing the window to 72x24 is precisely what works. The body's doc block is pin-scoped and accurate; the header is the one-line contract a future caller reads, and the block at `tui.c:1283-1292` explicitly contemplates one (the `smallwindow` branch "were it ever to want a size"), which is the caller that would be misled. Suggested fix: "FALSE where no oversize pin is to blame — including the plain too-small terminal, where growing does help — and the two outputs are then unset."

Nothing at blocker or should-fix severity.

## The two resolutions you flagged

I do not dispute either.

- **No LINES-axis "meeting the pin" arm.** Agreed. `tui_init()`'s oversize gate is `LINES > winsz.ws_row || COLS > winsz.ws_col` — one expression over both axes — and the retry site in `sst.c:689-693` is axis-blind; the axis-specific code (`pinned("LINES")` in `resize_term()` and in `axis_moved()`) is already reached by "pinned height", "pinned height unchanged" and "env size". A second full-game journey would re-prove a shared gate at real cost against a timeout already at 62%.
- **The `tui` timing note belonging to `CMakeLists.txt` and going to #101.** Correct under step 9: it is about code this diff does not touch, and filing is the answer there.

## The post-verifier edit

I accept it without another verifier round, and for a stronger reason than "it's only a comment": the edit is inside an `elif` chain where a misplaced comment would be a syntax error, and `sh -n` plus `shellcheck -s sh` both come back clean here, and I ran the whole file green against a binary built from the current sources. The verifier's earlier Debug *and* Release passes covered the arm's executable content unchanged.

## Review coverage

`ui-review` was owed — the diff adds a line the game prints — and you report two bound rounds with the current player-visible strings byte-identical to what round 2 exercised (the four advice forms and the size reports). I checked what I could: the diff's entire player-visible surface is those `proutf`/`prout` strings, all of which I reproduced live above, and the manual edits made after that round cannot reach a player *in game* — `helpme()` (`sst.c:169-200`) starts at a `  Mnemonic:` line and stops at the first line containing `******`, and the last such line before the changed block is `sst.doc:1471` (`********MODIFICATIONS********`), with no `Mnemonic:` entry after it. So the changed manual text is unreachable by `help`, and no fresh `ui-review` is owed for it.

## What I could not review

- The `ui-review` and `verifier` sessions themselves — I have only your account of their verdicts and coverage. My check is the one above: the strings they say they exercised are the strings the game prints today.
- The mutation proofs (`|| (pinned("COLUMNS") && COLS == winsz.ws_col)`, the `refusedtermcols` substitution, the dropped under-the-floor test). I did not re-run them. I did confirm each named arm exists and would in fact be the arm that breaks: "one pinned" runs `COLUMNS=80` in an 80-column pane, so the exact-match break takes its `want_quadtitle` down; the `needcols`→`refusedtermcols` break turns "both axes oversize" into `Grow to 100x40` and moves the "pinned axis" retry's 190; and dropping the floor test turns "oversize height with an undersize width" into `Grow to 100x40`, which I confirmed is wrong advice by running that env myself.
- macOS: the 512 clamp is measured on this machine's ncurses 6.6 only, and the 61-column bound is stated as resting on it. Only a nine-digit pin on both axes could exceed 72 without the clamp, so I am not raising it.

oversize, the notice offers the size the window would have to reach
beside the unset:

Grow to 190x30, or unset COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.
```

- The rerun rides with the **unset half alone**, because only that half

Four new arms in `tests/tui.sh`, each proved able to fail on a copy of

| `both axes oversize` | the only shape reaching the two-variable blame, and the widest line |

content.text:
Merged and done. #174 is closed, `main` is at `3286e1b`, and the branch is deleted both locally and on the remote.

## What shipped

A pin bigger than the window used to be answered with `Unset COLUMNS, rerun sst -t -- classic for now.` — advice that points away from the route both manuals promise. It now reads:

```
Terminal is 100x30 but LINES/COLUMNS make it 190x30.
Grow to 190x30, or unset COLUMNS and rerun sst -t.
```

The rerun attaches only to the unset half, since growing is answered at the next play-again in the same process. The size is the larger of pin and window per axis — not the pinned pair the report quotes, which in the tolerated-width case would tell the player to *narrow* a window already wide enough. Where a blamed axis is pinned under the floor, the unset-only wording stays, because no window is big enough there.

## What the review passes were actually worth

Six rounds of findings, and they were not ceremony:

- `ui-review` caught that "then rerun sst -t" told a player who grew the window to quit for nothing.
- `code-review` caught a comment that contradicted itself 19 lines later, and two successive versions of the `tui.h` contract that were each wrong about a different FALSE case.
- `verifier` caught that a promise I had just added to both manuals had no test — and writing that test exposed that my own first version counted the advice line, which a refused-but-unblamed retry never prints, so it would have passed with the panels down.

## Two things worth your attention

**Issue #180 is the one I would read.** Partway through, a text-mode editing script silently stripped the CRLF line endings from all 1130 lines of `sst.c`. A clean rebuild of both `ci-*` presets came back with byte-identical `.text` and zero warnings under `-Werror`; `ctest`, the journeys and the golden recordings all passed. Only `git diff --stat` noticed. Eleven source files are wholly CRLF and `.gitattributes` protects only the golden fixtures, so the same flip can arrive from any clone with `core.autocrlf=true`.

**Issue #101 has fresh numbers.** `tests/tui.sh` now runs 186.5s against its 300s timeout — 62% of the budget, up from the 68s that issue recorded. That is why I did not add a `LINES`-axis twin of the "meeting the pin" arm: the gate is one expression over both axes and the retry site is axis-blind, so a second full-game journey would re-prove shared code at real cost. That reasoning is in the PR body rather than left implicit.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "tui.c"
data = open(p, "rb").read().decode("latin-1")
old = """static void make_windows(void) {
	int msgh, statw, msgw, panelh, quadw;

	builtlines = LINES;
	builtcols = COLS;
"""
new = """/* The size the panels are laid out at: curses' screen, clipped to the
 * terminal's own wherever the two differ.
 *
 * They differ only under an exported LINES or COLUMNS. ncurses re-applies
 * that value in _nc_get_screensize() on every SIGWINCH, so a pinned axis
 * keeps its number however the window moves, and LINES and COLS then
 * describe a screen the player need not have. Laid out to those, the
 * panels are drawn off the edge: the status panel's right border and the
 * frame's corners land past the last column, and what is left wraps back
 * over the row above. Measured at COLUMNS=80 in a 100x30 pane dragged to
 * 70 columns.
 *
 * tui_init() refuses a pin bigger than the window at startup, so the
 * panels never start too big (#164). A pin no bigger than it is
 * tolerated, and the window can shrink under that afterwards, which is
 * the case this clips. #168.
 *
 * Clipped rather than stood down: both manuals say panels that are up
 * clip rather than give way to the classic display, and #94 has why --
 * ending curses under the player would be a worse answer to a mouse
 * drag. make_windows() already draws the panels as big as there is room
 * for rather than as big as they would like, so handing it the smaller
 * size is the whole of it.
 *
 * curses is left believing what it believes. Calling resize_term() to
 * the terminal's size would override a pin somebody set on purpose, and
 * ncurses would re-apply it at the next SIGWINCH regardless; the layout
 * is this file's to decide, and the pin is not.
 *
 * Where the ioctl has nothing to say, curses' numbers are all there is
 * -- the same fallback tui_init() makes. */
static void layout_size(int *rows, int *cols) {
	struct winsize ws;

	*rows = LINES;
	*cols = COLS;
	if (ioctl(fileno(stdout), TIOCGWINSZ, &ws) != 0 ||
	    ws.ws_row <= 0 || ws.ws_col <= 0)
		return;
	if (ws.ws_row < *rows) *rows = ws.ws_row;
	if (ws.ws_col < *cols) *cols = ws.ws_col;
}

static void make_windows(void) {
	int msgh, statw, msgw, panelh, quadw, rows, cols;

	layout_size(&rows, &cols);
	builtlines = rows;
	builtcols = cols;
"""
assert data.count(old) == 1
data = data.replace(old, new)

for a, b in [
    ("\tpanelh = LINES - MSGMIN;\n", "\tpanelh = rows - MSGMIN;\n"),
    ("\tif (panelh > LINES) panelh = LINES;\n", "\tif (panelh > rows) panelh = rows;\n"),
    ("\tquadw = COLS < QUADW ? COLS : QUADW;\n", "\tquadw = cols < QUADW ? cols : QUADW;\n"),
    ("\tmsgh = LINES - panelh > 1 ? LINES - panelh : 1;\n",
     "\tmsgh = rows - panelh > 1 ? rows - panelh : 1;\n"),
    ("\tstatw = COLS-QUADW > 1 ? COLS-QUADW : 1;\n",
     "\tstatw = cols-QUADW > 1 ? cols-QUADW : 1;\n"),
    ("\tmsgw = COLS-2 > 1 ? COLS-2 : 1;\n", "\tmsgw = cols-2 > 1 ? cols-2 : 1;\n"),
]:
    assert data.count(a) == 1, a
    data = data.replace(a, b)
open(p, "wb").write(data.encode("latin-1"))

 * is_term_resized() compares its arguments against the screen size
 * curses has cached, which is what LINES and COLS report. So this is
 * the same question as builtlines != LINES || builtcols != COLS for
 * the positive sizes make_windows() records -- not in general, since
 * is_term_resized() answers 0 for a non-positive argument whatever the
 * cache holds, measured: is_term_resized(0, 0) is 0 where the direct
 * comparison is 1. Those sizes cannot be non-positive by the time this
 * is asked: they are zero only before the first make_windows(), which
 * tui_init() runs before anything can reach sync_size(). Either way it
 * is answerable only once curses has processed the resize.
 *
 * Measured against ncurses 6.6.20251231, pane grown from 100x30 to
 * 120x40 with the windows built at the old size: before any curses
 * call LINES and COLS still read 100x30 and this answered 0; the first
 * doupdate() moved them to 120x40 and it answered 1. Asking
 * is_term_resized(LINES, COLS) instead would prove nothing either way
 * -- both sides come from the one cache, so it is 0 whatever the
 * terminal has done. #163. */
static int resized(void) {
	return is_term_resized(builtlines, builtcols);
}
"""
new = """/* Whether the layout size changed since the windows were built.
 *
 * The layout size and not curses' screen, which is the whole of what
 * this asks that is not obvious. It used to be is_term_resized(), which
 * compares against the size curses has cached -- the same question as
 * the direct comparison below for the positive sizes make_windows()
 * records, as long as the layout is curses' screen. Under a pin it is
 * not: a pinned axis never moves in that cache, however far the window
 * is dragged, so this answered no for the rest of the session and the
 * windows were never re-laid-out at all. That is the defect #168 is
 * about, and it is answered here rather than in make_windows() because
 * make_windows() is not reached until something says the size moved.
 *
 * Compared directly rather than through is_term_resized(), which can
 * only ask curses. builtlines and builtcols are positive by the time
 * this is asked -- they are zero only before the first make_windows(),
 * which tui_init() runs before anything can reach sync_size() -- and
 * layout_size() gives positive numbers, so the comparison has no
 * non-positive case to be careful about. That carefulness was the old
 * comment's subject: is_term_resized(0, 0) answers 0 where the direct
 * comparison answers 1, measured.
 *
 * On the unpinned axis it is still curses' number that decides, since
 * layout_size() clips rather than replaces, and curses has the new size
 * as soon as it processes the resize. Measured against ncurses
 * 6.6.20251231, pane grown from 100x30 to 120x40 with the windows built

 * layout_size() answers on the grow as well, but only the smaller of
 * the two is taken, so a grow is still noticed by curses catching up.
 * #163, #168. */
static int resized(void) {
	int rows, cols;

	layout_size(&rows, &cols);
	return rows != builtlines || cols != builtcols;
}

title:	README's resize section over-promises, then contradicts itself
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	
comments:	3
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	122
--
`README.md`'s "Full-screen mode" section promises more than the game does,
and then contradicts itself forty lines later.

## The over-promise

`README.md:19-21`:

> both the question you were asked and the answer you were halfway through
> typing survive, **so long as there is still room for them**

The room is not the condition. `restore_curline()` (`tui.c:402`) restores a
part-typed answer only when `curline` is non-empty — a prompt written with
`proutn`, which has not ended its line. A prompt written with `prout` ends its
own line, so `curlen` is 0 by the time the reader waits, and the function
takes its `curlen == 0` branch and returns at `tui.c:436` the moment
`pending_answer` is non-empty. Nothing is restored, however much room there
is.

Reproduced by `ui-review` at 80x24 with plenty of room to spare: the warp-time
question (`moving.c:594`, a `prout`), `y` typed and not entered, squeezed to
80x14. The surviving conversation row came back reading `Helmsman Sulu- "Warp
factor 1.0, Captain."` — old conversation — with the reader still holding the
invisible `y`.

`README.md:53-56` describes this correctly ("The one gap left is a question
you have already started answering"). So the file is internally inconsistent,
and the reassuring sentence is the one a player reads first.

Worth fixing together with the related correction now on #117: in that state a
resize loses *both* the question and the answer, not just the question.

## The over-generalization

`README.md:71-72`:

> answer `N` there and you are back at the prompt, free to give the command
> again

Not always. At `Do you want to play again?` (`sst.c:507-508`) `N` ends the
session, and there is no command to give again. The same sentence was written
into `sst.doc` for #113 and taken out again after `ui-review` raised it; the
manual now says only "answer N to decline whatever it was".

`README.md`'s "Full-screen mode" section promises more than the game does,
and then contradicts itself forty lines later.

## The over-promise

`README.md:19-21`:

> both the question you were asked and the answer you were halfway through
> typing survive, **so long as there is still room for them**

The room is not the condition. `restore_curline()` (`tui.c:402`) restores a
part-typed answer only when `curline` is non-empty — a prompt written with
`proutn`, which has not ended its line. A prompt written with `prout` ends its
own line, so `curlen` is 0 by the time the reader waits, and the function
takes its `curlen == 0` branch and returns at `tui.c:436` the moment
`pending_answer` is non-empty. Nothing is restored, however much room there
is.

Reproduced by `ui-review` at 80x24 with plenty of room to spare: the warp-time
question (`moving.c:594`, a `prout`), `y` typed and not entered, squeezed to
80x14. The surviving conversation row came back reading `Helmsman Sulu- "Warp
factor 1.0, Captain."` — old conversation — with the reader still holding the
invisible `y`.

`README.md:53-56` describes this correctly ("The one gap left is a question
you have already started answering"). So the file is internally inconsistent,
and the reassuring sentence is the one a player reads first.

Worth fixing together with the related correction now on #117: in that state a
resize loses *both* the question and the answer, not just the question.

## The over-generalization

`README.md:71-72`:

> answer `N` there and you are back at the prompt, free to give the command
> again

Not always. At `Do you want to play again?` (`sst.c:507-508`) `N` ends the
session, and there is no command to give again. The same sentence was written
into `sst.doc` for #113 and taken out again after `ui-review` raised it; the
manual now says only "answer N to decline whatever it was".

content.text: A race, not a defect: `want_quadtitle` passes as soon as the title is back, which is before the redraw settles. Replacing the one-shot checks with a polling helper:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "tests/tui.sh"
data = open(p, "rb").read().decode("latin-1")

# 1. helper, next to uniform_col which it sits beside in purpose
anchor = "uniform_col() {\n"
assert data.count(anchor) == 1
helper = '''# Wait until each of the first $2 rows is exactly $1 characters wide.
# That is how a panel row reads when its right border is the last thing
# on it: capture-pane strips trailing blanks, so a row measures the
# panel's width only if something is drawn in that column, and on these
# rows that something is the border. A panel left wider than the window
# comes back ragged instead, each row stopping wherever its own text
# ran out.
#
# Polled rather than asked once, because a resize and the redraw that
# answers it are two events and the game is between them for a moment.
# want_quadtitle is not enough to separate them: the title comes back
# with the first repaint, where the width comes back with the relayout.
# Asked once, the grow half of the "pin shrink" arm failed against a
# build that was drawing it correctly a fraction of a second later.
wait_panel_width() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | awk -v w="$1" -v n="$2" '
			NR <= n { if (length($0) != w) bad = 1 }
			END { exit (bad || NR < n) }' && return 0
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

'''
data = data.replace(anchor, helper + anchor)

# 2. both checks use it
old_shrink = '''\t\tif ! screen | awk 'NR <= 13 { if (length($0) != 70) bad = 1 }
\t\t                   END { exit (bad || NR < 13) }'; then
\t\t\tfail "pin shrink: the panels stayed wider than the window they are on"
'''
new_shrink = '''\t\tif ! wait_panel_width 70 13; then
\t\t\tfail "pin shrink: the panels stayed wider than the window they are on"
'''
assert data.count(old_shrink) == 1
data = data.replace(old_shrink, new_shrink)

old_grow = '''\t\t\tif ! screen | awk 'NR <= 13 { if (length($0) != 80) bad = 1 }
\t\t\t                   END { exit (bad || NR < 13) }'; then
\t\t\t\tfail "pin shrink: widening did not restore the panels to the pin"
'''
new_grow = '''\t\t\tif ! wait_panel_width 80 13; then
\t\t\t\tfail "pin shrink: widening did not restore the panels to the pin"
'''
assert data.count(old_grow) == 1
data = data.replace(old_grow, new_grow)
open(p, "wb").write(data.encode("latin-1"))
print("ok")
PY
sh -n tests/tui.sh && shellcheck -s sh tests/tui.sh && echo "shellcheck clean"

input.prompt:
Read .claude/agents/ui-review.md and follow it. Review the working tree of /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek on branch fix/pin-overflow-on-resize (all changes uncommitted; `git diff main` shows the whole change). The debug build at build/debug/sst is current with the working tree.

**What the change does (issue #168).** An exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` no bigger than the window is deliberately tolerated — the panels are drawn narrow or short with room to spare. But ncurses re-applies that pinned value on every SIGWINCH, so a pinned axis never moves in curses' cache, and the layout asked curses. Shrink the window under such a pin and nothing was re-laid-out: the panels stayed at the pin's size, drawn off the edge of the screen they were on. Measured before the fix, `COLUMNS=80` in a 100x30 pane dragged to 70 columns — the status panel's right border and the frame's corners were past the last column and the rows came back ragged (70, 30, 51, 50 characters where all thirteen should end alike). Both manuals promised clipping and then carried an "except under a pin" clause admitting they did not.

The fix adds `layout_size()` in `tui.c` — curses' screen clipped to the terminal's own via `TIOCGWINSZ` — and lays the windows out to that instead of `LINES`/`COLS`. `resized()` now compares against the layout size rather than asking `is_term_resized()`, which could only ever ask curses. Both manuals lose the "except under a pin" exception.

Deliberate choices worth your judgement:

- **Clip, not stand down.** Both manuals say panels that are up clip rather than give way to the classic display, and #94 argues ending curses under a player is a worse answer to a mouse drag. `make_windows()` already draws panels as big as there is room for, so handing it the smaller size is the whole of it.
- **curses is left believing the pin.** No `resize_term()` to the terminal's size — that would override a value somebody set on purpose, and ncurses would re-apply it at the next SIGWINCH anyway.
- **The clip is not a latch.** Widening past the pin again restores the panels to the pin's size, not the window's, since `layout_size()` takes the smaller of the two.

Please look hard at what the player actually sees: the shrink, the widen back, whether the narrowed panels clip their contents legibly (the `>` marker the manuals promise for a line with more to show), what happens at and below the 72-column minimum under a pin, what a *height* pin does when the window gets shorter (the arm I added covers width only), and whether the reworded manual paragraphs match the behaviour. Reproduce with tmux on your own socket (`-L`, `-f /dev/null`), e.g. `tmux -f /dev/null -L uirev new-session -d -x 100 -y 30 -s t 'env COLUMNS=80 ./build/debug/sst -t tournament 7 short novice pw; sleep 60'` then `resize-window -t t -x 70 -y 30`.

Report findings only; do not edit files.

content.text:
Cleaned up my tmux socket (`-L uirev`) and the scratch build. Findings below.

## 1. Verdict

**Needs changes.** The core of the change is right and visibly works: under `COLUMNS=80` in a 100-column pane dragged to 70, the panels now come down to 70 and every one of the thirteen panel rows ends on the last column, the `>` clip marker still appears where a status line runs out of room (verified at 74, 70, 60 and 40 columns), widening back restores them to the pin's 80 rather than the window's 100, a resize during a pause still redraws, and a height pin shrunk in one step lays out correctly at 24, 18, 16, 14, 13, 12, 10 and 8 rows. But one line that the change did not update now reads curses' width where it needs the layout width, and the result is a **duplicated half-typed command line** in exactly the scenario the change ships for. There is also a second, pre-existing artifact on the height axis that the reworded manuals now claim parity for and don't have: a *dragged* (multi-step) height shrink under a pin scrolls the real terminal, permanently loses the panels' top border and titles, and does not heal when the window grows back. One added line fixes both residuals; I verified both fixes on a copy outside the repository.

## 2. Findings

### Blocker — `tui.c:1076`: a pinned width shrink stamps a second copy of the player's unfinished line

`sync_size()` still asks `restore_curline(COLS != oldcols ? oldcols - 2 : 0)`. `oldcols` is now the *layout* width (`builtcols`), but `COLS` is curses' width, which under a pin never moves — so on the first shrink past the pin the test reads "the width did not change" when it did, `restore_curline()` takes the height-only branch (`tui.c:949`), scrolls, and rewrites the line under the truncated stump.

What a player sees (reproduced: `COLUMNS=80`, 100x30 pane, 62 characters typed at ` COMMAND>`, pane resized to 70x30 — a tmux resize, a pane zoom toggle, or a window-manager maximize/restore, i.e. any jump rather than a smooth drag):

```
28 [ 69]  COMMAND> REDACTED
29 [ 69]  COMMAND> REDACTED
30 [  4]  hij
```

Row 28 is the stale stump; the scroll that made room for the rewrite also cost a row of conversation. The cursor lands correctly (typing `XYZ` appends to row 30), so it is cosmetic — but it is precisely the stacking artifact `restore_curline()` exists to prevent (#117, #118), it is **new on this branch** (`main` under the same pin leaves a single line, because it never re-laid-out at all), and the unpinned control at the same drag is clean.

Suggestion: compare the layout width, `restore_curline(builtcols != oldcols ? oldcols - 2 : 0);`. I applied exactly that to a copy of the branch outside the repo, rebuilt, and the duplicate is gone on the shrink and the full line comes back on the widen. Note the new test arm in `tests/tui.sh` types nothing at the prompt, so it passes with this bug present — worth typing a line longer than the post-shrink message width before the resize.

### Should-fix — height pin: a real drag loses the panel headings for good, and the manuals now promise it doesn't

`README.md:135-137` and `sst.doc:1588-1591` now say panels "clip rather than give way to the classic display, under a pin as much as without one". On the width axis that holds. On the height axis it does not once there is more than one shrink step below the pin — which is what a mouse drag is:

`env LINES=30`, pane 100x40, dragged 38→36→34→32→30→28→26→24 (ending at a size the game accepts at startup):

```
 1 x  3  . . . . . . . . . .   xx Position      3
...
 9 mqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqjmqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqq
11  a deadly Klingon invasion force. As captain o
12  a deadly Klingon invasion force. As captain o
```

The top border and both panel titles are gone, a conversation line is duplicated, further `srscan`s do not repair it, and **growing the window back to 40 rows does not repair it either** — which contradicts `README.md:43-45` ("Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the squeeze went"). Minimal repro: 40→34→28→24, or 40→26→24; 40→24 in one step and 40→30→24 are both clean, so the trigger is a shrink step taken while already clipped. `LINES=24` at 30→20→14 shows the same. Same drag with no pin is perfect. This is *not* a regression — `main` under the same drag is worse (it loses four more rows) — but the reworded sentence is what brings it into this change's scope.

Cause: curses still believes the pinned height, so its stdscr is taller than the physical screen and the terminal scrolls under it; ncurses' image never learns, so nothing repaints the rows that scrolled.

Suggestion: one line in `sync_size()`, `clearok(curscr, TRUE);` right after `make_windows()`. I tested it on the copy: the 40→34→28→24 drag comes back with the frame, titles and prompt intact, the unpinned journeys and the pinned width shrink/widen are unchanged, and it also cleans up finding 3 below. If you would rather not repaint the whole screen on every resize step, the alternative is to narrow the manuals' claim to the width axis and file the height case as an issue — but the parity sentence as written should not ship with the behavior as it is.

### Nit — very narrow pinned widths render worse than unpinned

Pinned `COLUMNS=80` dragged to 30 columns leaves rows 2-12 one column short (the status panel's single-column right border missing, row 13 two short); at 20 columns each panel row is shifted, the left border gone and the grid's first columns replaced by blanks — where the unpinned display at the same widths is exactly right. Deep clip territory well under 72 columns, so low priority, and the `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` above makes the pinned 20-column screen identical to the unpinned one.

### Nit — the new test arm covers width only

`tests/tui.sh` gains a width arm with a good comment; there is no height arm, and the height axis is the one with the residual above. If finding 2 is fixed, a stepwise `40→34→28→24` height arm asserting the top border row is present would lock it in.

### Nit — `sst.doc:1583-1586` wraps awkwardly

## 3. What I exercised

**What the change does (issue #168).** An exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` no bigger than the window is deliberately tolerated — the panels are drawn narrow or short with room to spare. But ncurses re-applies that pinned value on every SIGWINCH, so a pinned axis never moves in curses' cache, and the layout asked curses. Shrink the window under such a pin and nothing was re-laid-out: the panels stayed at the pin's size, drawn off the edge of the screen they were on. Measured before the fix, `COLUMNS=80` in a 100x30 pane dragged to 70 columns — the status panel's right border and the frame's corners were past the last column and the rows came back ragged (70, 30, 51, 50 characters where all thirteen should end alike). Both manuals promised clipping and then carried an "except under a pin" clause admitting they did not.

The fix adds `layout_size()` in `tui.c` — curses' screen clipped to the terminal's own via `TIOCGWINSZ` — and lays the windows out to that instead of `LINES`/`COLS`. `resized()` now compares against the layout size rather than asking `is_term_resized()`, which could only ever ask curses. Both manuals lose the "except under a pin" exception.

Deliberate choices worth your judgement:

- **Clip, not stand down.** Both manuals say panels that are up clip rather than give way to the classic display, and #94 argues ending curses under a player is a worse answer to a mouse drag. `make_windows()` already draws panels as big as there is room for, so handing it the smaller size is the whole of it.
- **curses is left believing the pin.** No `resize_term()` to the terminal's size — that would override a value somebody set on purpose, and ncurses would re-apply it at the next SIGWINCH anyway.
- **The clip is not a latch.** Widening past the pin again restores the panels to the pin's size, not the window's, since `layout_size()` takes the smaller of the two.

Cleaned up my tmux socket (`-L uirev`) and the scratch build. Findings below.

## 1. Verdict

**Needs changes.** The core of the change is right and visibly works: under `COLUMNS=80` in a 100-column pane dragged to 70, the panels now come down to 70 and every one of the thirteen panel rows ends on the last column, the `>` clip marker still appears where a status line runs out of room (verified at 74, 70, 60 and 40 columns), widening back restores them to the pin's 80 rather than the window's 100, a resize during a pause still redraws, and a height pin shrunk in one step lays out correctly at 24, 18, 16, 14, 13, 12, 10 and 8 rows. But one line that the change did not update now reads curses' width where it needs the layout width, and the result is a **duplicated half-typed command line** in exactly the scenario the change ships for. There is also a second, pre-existing artifact on the height axis that the reworded manuals now claim parity for and don't have: a *dragged* (multi-step) height shrink under a pin scrolls the real terminal, permanently loses the panels' top border and titles, and does not heal when the window grows back. One added line fixes both residuals; I verified both fixes on a copy outside the repository.

## 2. Findings

### Blocker — `tui.c:1076`: a pinned width shrink stamps a second copy of the player's unfinished line

`sync_size()` still asks `restore_curline(COLS != oldcols ? oldcols - 2 : 0)`. `oldcols` is now the *layout* width (`builtcols`), but `COLS` is curses' width, which under a pin never moves — so on the first shrink past the pin the test reads "the width did not change" when it did, `restore_curline()` takes the height-only branch (`tui.c:949`), scrolls, and rewrites the line under the truncated stump.

What a player sees (reproduced: `COLUMNS=80`, 100x30 pane, 62 characters typed at ` COMMAND>`, pane resized to 70x30 — a tmux resize, a pane zoom toggle, or a window-manager maximize/restore, i.e. any jump rather than a smooth drag):

```
28 [ 69]  COMMAND> REDACTED
29 [ 69]  COMMAND> REDACTED
30 [  4]  hij
```

Row 28 is the stale stump; the scroll that made room for the rewrite also cost a row of conversation. The cursor lands correctly (typing `XYZ` appends to row 30), so it is cosmetic — but it is precisely the stacking artifact `restore_curline()` exists to prevent (#117, #118), it is **new on this branch** (`main` under the same pin leaves a single line, because it never re-laid-out at all), and the unpinned control at the same drag is clean.

Suggestion: compare the layout width, `restore_curline(builtcols != oldcols ? oldcols - 2 : 0);`. I applied exactly that to a copy of the branch outside the repo, rebuilt, and the duplicate is gone on the shrink and the full line comes back on the widen. Note the new test arm in `tests/tui.sh` types nothing at the prompt, so it passes with this bug present — worth typing a line longer than the post-shrink message width before the resize.

### Should-fix — height pin: a real drag loses the panel headings for good, and the manuals now promise it doesn't

`README.md:135-137` and `sst.doc:1588-1591` now say panels "clip rather than give way to the classic display, under a pin as much as without one". On the width axis that holds. On the height axis it does not once there is more than one shrink step below the pin — which is what a mouse drag is:

`env LINES=30`, pane 100x40, dragged 38→36→34→32→30→28→26→24 (ending at a size the game accepts at startup):

```
 1 x  3  . . . . . . . . . .   xx Position      3
...
 9 mqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqjmqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqq
11  a deadly Klingon invasion force. As captain o
12  a deadly Klingon invasion force. As captain o
```

The top border and both panel titles are gone, a conversation line is duplicated, further `srscan`s do not repair it, and **growing the window back to 40 rows does not repair it either** — which contradicts `README.md:43-45` ("Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the squeeze went"). Minimal repro: 40→34→28→24, or 40→26→24; 40→24 in one step and 40→30→24 are both clean, so the trigger is a shrink step taken while already clipped. `LINES=24` at 30→20→14 shows the same. Same drag with no pin is perfect. This is *not* a regression — `main` under the same drag is worse (it loses four more rows) — but the reworded sentence is what brings it into this change's scope.

Cause: curses still believes the pinned height, so its stdscr is taller than the physical screen and the terminal scrolls under it; ncurses' image never learns, so nothing repaints the rows that scrolled.

Suggestion: one line in `sync_size()`, `clearok(curscr, TRUE);` right after `make_windows()`. I tested it on the copy: the 40→34→28→24 drag comes back with the frame, titles and prompt intact, the unpinned journeys and the pinned width shrink/widen are unchanged, and it also cleans up finding 3 below. If you would rather not repaint the whole screen on every resize step, the alternative is to narrow the manuals' claim to the width axis and file the height case as an issue — but the parity sentence as written should not ship with the behavior as it is.

### Nit — very narrow pinned widths render worse than unpinned

Pinned `COLUMNS=80` dragged to 30 columns leaves rows 2-12 one column short (the status panel's single-column right border missing, row 13 two short); at 20 columns each panel row is shifted, the left border gone and the grid's first columns replaced by blanks — where the unpinned display at the same widths is exactly right. Deep clip territory well under 72 columns, so low priority, and the `clearok(curscr, TRUE)` above makes the pinned 20-column screen identical to the unpinned one.

### Nit — the new test arm covers width only

`tests/tui.sh` gains a width arm with a good comment; there is no height arm, and the height axis is the one with the residual above. If finding 2 is fixed, a stepwise `40→34→28→24` height arm asserting the top border row is present would lock it in.

### Nit — `sst.doc:1583-1586` wraps awkwardly

"…but the display stops believing it past the size you actually / have." leaves `have.` alone on a line. Cosmetic; the file has other short tails. Both paragraphs are within 80 columns and keep the file's CRLF, and the prose reads in the game's voice.

input.command:

p = "tui.c"

"""
new = """	make_windows();		/* which is what moves builtlines/builtcols on */
	/* Repaint the screen rather than the difference, because under a
	   pin ncurses' idea of what is on the terminal can be wrong and
	   it has no way to find out. Its stdscr is the pinned size, so on
	   a pinned axis it believes in rows or columns the player does not
	   have; the terminal scrolls under it as text arrives, and the
	   optimiser then leaves alone every cell it thinks is already

	   Cheap where it is asked: this is reached only when the layout
	   size actually moved, which is a human dragging a window. #168. */
	clearok(curscr, TRUE);
"""
assert data.count(old) == 1
open(p, "wb").write(data.replace(old, new).encode("latin-1"))

content.text: The arm's indentation is one tab, and typing a pending line would collide with the `srscan` that follows. Cleaner as two separate arms:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "tests/tui.sh"
data = open(p, "rb").read().decode("latin-1")
anchor = "# --- a resize during a pause redraws without waiting for the player ---\n"
assert data.count(anchor) == 1
arms = '''# --- and the pending line is not stacked when the pin hides the shrink -
# sync_size() decides whether to put a half-typed line back from whether
# the width moved, and it asked COLS. Under a pin COLS never moves, so a
# shrink past the pin read as height-only: restore_curline() took that
# branch, scrolled, and left a truncated copy of the line above the
# rewritten one -- the stacking it exists to prevent (#117, #118),
# arriving by the door layout_size() opened. Found by ui-review on this
# branch, against the arm above, which types nothing and so passed
# straight through it. #168.
#
# 62 characters, so the line wraps at 70 and a stump cannot be mistaken
# for an intact line. Typed and not entered: the defect is in what a
# resize does to a line still being composed.
start 100 30 'tournament 7 short novice pw' 'env COLUMNS=80'
if ! to_command; then
\tfail "pin pending: the game never reached its command prompt"
\tdump
else
\ttm send-keys -t "$pane" \\
\t\t'REDACTED'
\ttm resize-window -t "$session" -x 70 -y 30
\tif ! wait_pane '#{pane_width}' 70; then
\t\tfail "pin pending: the terminal never narrowed, so nothing was tested"
\t\tdump
\telif ! wait_for 'REDACTED'; then
\t\tfail "pin pending: the half-typed command did not survive the shrink"
\t\tdump
\telif [ "$(screen | grep -c 'REDACTED')" -ne 1 ]; then
\t\tfail "pin pending: the half-typed command was left stacked"
\t\tdump
\tfi
fi

# --- a dragged height shrink under a pin keeps its frame ---------------
# A mouse drag is many small shrinks, not one big one, and under a pin
# that is the case that broke. curses believes the pinned height, so its
# stdscr is taller than the screen the player has; the terminal scrolls
# under it as text arrives and ncurses' image never learns, so the
# optimiser leaves alone the cells it thinks are already right --
# including the ones that scrolled away. The panels' top border and both
# titles went, and came back neither on the next command nor on growing
# the window again.
#
# 40 -> 34 -> 28 -> 24 with LINES=30, which is the shape that does it: a
# single 40 -> 24 is clean, so it is a shrink taken while already
# clipped. 24 rows is a size the game accepts at startup, so nothing
# here is about being too small. Found by ui-review on this branch,
# against manual text this change had just reworded to promise parity
# between the axes. Fixed by clearok(curscr, TRUE) in sync_size(). #168.
#
# want_quadtitle is the whole assertion: it reads the top row for a
# coordinate-bearing title, which is exactly the border row that went.
start 100 40 'tournament 7 short novice pw' 'env LINES=30'
if ! to_command; then
\tfail "pin drag: the game never reached its command prompt"
\tdump
else
\tdragged=1
\tfor h in 34 28 24; do
\t\ttm resize-window -t "$session" -x 100 -y "$h"
\t\tif ! wait_pane '#{pane_height}' "$h"; then
\t\t\tfail "pin drag: the terminal never reached $h rows"
\t\t\tdump
\t\t\tdragged=0
\t\t\tbreak
\t\tfi
\tdone
\tif [ "$dragged" -eq 1 ]; then
\t\ttm send-keys -t "$pane" 'srscan' Enter
\t\twant_quadtitle "pin drag: a dragged shrink under a pin lost the panel frame"
\tfi
fi

'''
open(p, "wb").write(data.replace(anchor, arms + anchor).encode("latin-1"))
print("ok")
PY
sh -n tests/tui.sh && shellcheck -s sh tests/tui.sh && echo "shellcheck clean"

content.content:
ok
  Only a pin the panels can live with is left alone: no bigger than
  your window and still 72x24 or more, where they are drawn narrow or
  short with room to spare. Shrink the window below such a pin and
  the panels come down with it: the pin does not follow the window
  down, but the display stops believing it past the size you have.

  It only goes that way. Panels that are up stay up for the rest of
  the session however you resize the terminal: they clip rather than
  give way to the classic display, under a pin as much as without
  one.

  Resizing the terminal never crashes the game and never drops it back
  to the classic display, at any point, including while the game waits
  for an answer or for a keystroke at a pause. It can still cost you
  one of the two -- the question you were part way through answering,
  or on a very wide terminal the answer itself -- which is what the
  last of these paragraphs is about. Resizing is safe in that classic
  display too: it neither answers a question nor turns a page for you,
  and what you had already typed is still there.

  Narrower than 72 columns, the panel lines clip rather than wrap,
  and a line with more to show than there is room for ends in ">",
  so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small one. Shorter, it
  is the panels that give up lines: they lose rows off the bottom, the
  scan keeping its numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and
  the conversation keeps three rows down to six -- two of it and the
  line the prompt or the pager sits on. Below six there is not that
  much left to divide and it keeps what there is, two rows at five and
  one at four. So the prompt is on screen down to four rows, and down
  to six a paged command shows a line of itself before stopping to ask
  -- at five its one line goes to the blank that LRSCAN, CHART and
  STATUS open with, though SRSCAN, which has none, still shows a line
  there, and at four the pager takes the only row and a paged command
  shows nothing of itself at all. None of this is a crash, however
  cramped or dead the screen looks.

  Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it however far
  the squeeze went, since they redraw from the game state. The
  conversation does not come back that way, and a line that was cut
  short stays cut short. Little goes with it: SRSCAN, LRSCAN,
  STATUS, CHART and DAMAGES all cost nothing and can be asked again,
  and the chart shows where the starbases are from the start,
  briefing or no briefing. What is gone is whatever the game said
  only once -- how hard the last salvo hit you, what your torpedo
  did.

  The line you were on usually comes back with the panels, and so does
  whatever you had typed of an answer to it -- but look at both before
  you touch the keyboard, because you may get back only one of them.
  Where the question ended its own line, your answer starts the row
  below it, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a window of one
  or two -- five rows or fewer -- cannot hold the pair; a question
  that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is what
  goes, leaving you looking at what you typed with nothing on screen
  to say what it answers; on a very wide terminal it is the answer
  that goes instead, however tall the window is, leaving a question
  that looks as though nothing had been typed at all. Shorter still
  and only a piece of whichever survived is left, and sometimes
  neither comes back, leaving older conversation on screen with the
  game waiting behind it. If the question and all you had typed are
  both on screen, carry on. If either is missing, give the terminal
  another row or two before anything else: that usually brings it back
  with your typing untouched, which beats retyping it -- the
  self-destruct password can be nine characters. A very wide terminal
  is the exception: more rows will not bring the answer back there,
  though making it narrow enough will. If it does not come back, or
  the terminal cannot grow, do not answer and do not press Enter:
  press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away. What you typed is
  still in it unseen, and a yes/no question reads the first word of
  your answer and only its first letter, so an "N" typed after a "y"
  you cannot see answers yes -- and some of those questions can end
  the game. With the line cleared, Enter is safe, since nothing
  waiting behind a prompt commits you to anything. A yes/no question
  then asks again only as Please answer with "Y" or "N", never
  repeating what it wanted; answer N to decline whatever it was.


                ----------ACKNOWLEDGMENTS----------                    27

The authors would like to thank Professor Michael Duggan for his
encouragement and administrative assistance with the development of
the Star Trek game, without which it might never have been completed.

Much credit is due to Patrick McGehearty and Rich Cohen, who assisted
with the original design of the game and contributed greatly to its
conceptual development.

Thanks are also due to Carl Strange, Hardy Tichenor and Steven Bruell
for their assistance with certain coding problems.

This game was inspired by and rather loosely based on an earlier
game, programmed in the BASIC language, by Jim Korp and Grady Hicks.
It is the authors' understanding that the BASIC game was in turn
derived from a still earlier version in use at Penn State University.




                 ----------REFERENCES----------


 1.  "Star Trek" (the original television series), produced and
     directed by Gene Rodenberry.

 2.  "Star Trek" (the animated television series), produced by Gene
     Rodenberry and directed by Hal Sutherland.  Also excellent,
     and not just kiddie fare.  If you enjoyed the original series
     you should enjoy this one (unless you have some sort of a
     hangup about watching cartoons).

 3.  "The Making of Star Trek", by Steven E. Whitfield and Gene
     Rodenberry.  The best and most complete readily available
     book about Star Trek.  (Ballantine Books)

 4.  "The World of Star Trek", by David Gerrold.  Similiar in scope
     to the above book.  (Bantam)

 5.  "The Star Trek Guide", third revision 4/17/67, by Gene
     Rodenberry.  The original writer's guide for the television
     series, but less comprehensive than (3) above.
     (Norway Productions)

 6.  "The Trouble With Tribbles", by David Gerrold.  Includes the
     complete script of this popular show.  (Ballantine Books)

 7.  "Star Trek", "Star Trek 2", ..., "Star Trek 9", by James Blish.
     The original shows in short story form.  (Bantam)

 8.  "Spock Must Die", by James Blish.  An original novel, but
     rather similar to the show "The Enemy Within".  (Bantam)

 9.  Model kits of the Enterprise and a "Klingon Battle-Cruiser"
     by AMT Corporation are available at most hobby shops.
